Hamilton’s Mechanical River, the Deadleg Wobblers, the Palmetto Choral Collective Peace Choir and ormer Charleston poet laureate Marcus Amaker. The series was organized by the Charleston Climate Coalition, the M.A.R.S.H. Project and Microdose Cooperative. For Belvin Olasov, director and co- ounder o the Charleston Climate Coalition, the series represents an oppor- tunity to bring the spirit o the olk-protest movements o the 1960s into a contempo- rary environmental fght. “I’m someone who is really interested in the use o music in countercultural protest movements,” Olasov said. “There was a time when music and art and culture were just more naturally interconnected with change-making activism causes.” Inspired by that connection, Olasov wanted to bring that tradition to the Lowcountry. The series has taken dierent orms, rom a coee shop to a pool, but attendance has grown steadily, and now the series moves to Music Farm or its fnale. Music and climate action The cause behind the concerts is a proposed $5 billion natural gas-fred power plant near Canadys in Colleton County along the Edisto River. Dominion Energy South Carolina and state-owned Santee Cooper plan to jointly develop the 2,200-megawatt acility, which received approval rom the S.C. Public Service Commission in May. The project also involves a new natural gas pipeline and its inrastructure, which raises concerns about impacts on the ACE Basin, one o the Lowcountry’s signifcant natural landscapes. Environmental advocates ques- tion the project’s cost, air pollution, water quality and the long-term consequences o expanding ossil uel inrastructure. For Olasov and the Charleston Climate Coalition, the convergence o the gas plant, pipeline and data center development rep- resents an especially troubling moment or the region. The coalition has spent seven years advocating or climate action in the Lowcountry, including clean energy, green buildings and public transportation. “In my time as a climate activist, there hasn’t been any ashpoint as dangerous as this gas plant,” Olasov said. The concerts oer a way to make that fght more visible while giving people an accessible entry point into environmental activism. “The idea was to create some sort o conuence o energy, something that brings people together to a cause bigger than themselves,” he said. That sense o community and enjoyment is particularly important when the issues themselves can eel overwhelming. “The nature o the issue is dark,” Olasov said. “This ossil uel inrastructure is or data centers, not or us. So I think bal- ancing out that darkness with lightness and energy is really important.” A creative collaboration The Charleston Climate Coalition has worked with the M.A.R.S.H. Project or several years, fnding common ground in an approach to environmental advocacy. The M.A.R.S.H. Project is a Charleston- based environmental initiative that com- bines ecological stewardship and community engagement with creative activism to protect the Lowcountry’s natural environment. Microdose Cooperative is a creative com- munity organization that collaborates on arts and music events, helping bring projects such as Songs To Save The Edisto to lie. “They share a lot o the same ideals o cen- tralizing joy and play and creativity, as well as love and reverence or our natural world,” Olasov said. “To me, the joy o this work is in the collaboration and great people you get to work with and to be riends with,” Olasov said. “To me, this series couldn’t have hap- pened without the M.A.R.S.H. Project and Microdose Cooperative.” Although Nov. 4 marks the end o the series, Olasov sees potential or the ormat to support other environmental causes, including wider use o solar energy and creating protected bike lanes in downtown Charleston. “I won’t say that the climate activist’s job is never fnished because one day, we simply must be fnished,” Olasov said. “But there is a lot o work to do between now and then.” IF YOU WANT TO GO: Doors open at 7 p.m, Nov. 4., Music Farm, 32 Ann St., Charleston. Tickets range from $24-$44. musicfarm.com.
